docs.text: e02: Jus the two functions //e02: pulls the apogee prediction out into its own sketch (two recursive functions) so the calc time can be measured const float airDensity = 1.297; // density in kg/m^3 const float referenceArea = .038; // m/2 const float mass = .619; // mass of rocket in kg 😊 const float dragCoeficciant = 1.31; // in a number void setup() { // put your setup code here, to run once: Serial.begin(9600); } void loop() { float height = 200; float time_0 = pTime(); float velocity = 8.7374; for (int i = 0; i<1; i++) { height += getDeltaHeight_together(height, velocity, 0.073, 0); height += getDeltaHeight_seperated(height, velocity, 1.32); } Serial.println((String)height); Serial.println(pTime()-time_0); delay(1000); } float getDeltaHeight_seperated(float height, float velocity, float dragCoeficciant) { if (velocity < 1) { return 0.0; } float force = .5 * dragCoeficciant * 0.038 /*referenceArea*/ * airDensity * velocity * velocity; float acceleration = force / 0.619 /*mass*/; velocity -= acceleration * .25; float delta_height = 0; delta_height = delta_height + velocity * .25 + getDeltaHeight_seperated(height, velocity, 1.32); return delta_height; } float getDeltaHeight_together(float height, float velocity, float dragCoeficciant, float time) { if (time >= .71) { return 0.0; } float force = .5 * dragCoeficciant * 0.038 /*referenceArea*/ * airDensity * velocity * velocity; float acceleration = force / 0.619 /*mass*/; velocity -= acceleration * .05; time += .05; float delta_height = 0; delta_height = delta_height + velocity * .05 + getDeltaHeight_together(height, velocity, .073, time); return delta_height; } double pTime() { return ((double)(millis())) / (double)(1000); }

docs.text: General Overview The project has been in the works for about a month or so now. The initial problem that needed to be solved was to control descent of the rocket to within the designated threshold by ARC (the last year was 36-39s). Our previous solution to controlling descent time was to place a zip tie progressively higher up on the parachute shroud lines, which should reduce the amount the parachute opens up and therefore increase descent time. However, a huge factor at play is sudden gusts of wind, which messed with our final qualification flight - we had a launch with perfect time of descent, and then reefed the parachute MORE, and then the time of descent increased. This means that the time of descent must be controlled onboard the rocket, instead of hoping to get lucky with weather. Thus, the idea of dynamic reefing came about. Conceptual Solution The current theoretical solution thus far has been threading a Kevlar string (typically used for shock cord) around the circumference of the parachute, and then winching in that string with a servo onboard the rocket in order to effectively decrease circumference of the parachute → lowering surface area → decreasing descent time. This would then be controlled by the onboard avionics which would attempt to predict, after a few seconds of coasting, if the rocket will touch down to the ground at the required time (safely). There will likely be a ‘hard stop’ in the code which will prevent the rocket from shattering upon descent. Current Steps The current step in development is creating an overkill proof of concept. A simple payload with space for a 27 kg/cm servo (which in itself weighs approx 70g, quite heavy for our needs) has been CADded and printed out of lightweight PLA. The winch went through multiple iterations, starting with an ellipsoidal cross section a few times before I realized that it would result in uneven thread pull, before finally landing on a spool thread-like design (after further reflection, this makes by far the most sense and it is strange that I decided against it initially). 35 kg/cm servo, quite strong Crude prototype of reefing mechanism The first parachute attached was a bog standard 18” ripstock nylon parachute made by Apogee. Using the basic formula for terminal velocity (vt = √(2mg / (pACd)), plugging in standard values for p (air density, 1.225 kg/m³) and Cd (standard drag coefficient, 1.5) for a hemispherical parachute, a mass of approximately 240g, and approximating projected surface area to be around 0.7x of total surface area, we get a vt of (√((2 * 0.240kg * 9.81m/s2)/(1.225 kg/m³ * 0.115 m2 * 1.5)) = 4.72 m/s. This was accurately depicted in our drop tests of the payload with such a parachute, in which we realized that we would have very little window to determine any modulations in descent time with the reefing. We thus decided on making our own makeshift parachutes - ordering every time we need a different size from Apogee takes at least several weeks, and we would be able to customize the diameter perfectly. Our first parachute was made out of Amazon ‘kite’ nylon with a 40cm radius, quadrupling surface area from our previous 46cm DIAMETER parachute and thus reducing terminal velocity by a factor of 2. Our custom parachute made out of lightweight nylon Grommets are used along the circumference of the parachute for both attachment of shroud lines and threading of the reefing line. One noticeable concern as of now is the management of different lines - even in the small scale 18” parachute there was considerable entanglement of the shroud and reefing lines. This will likely be the most difficult issue to deal with, as the line management will only get more complex as we move from this prototype to enstating the same system within a body tube of a narrow rocket at an imperfect orientation. Example of the difficulties with reefing and shrouding lines. They can get very tangled very quickly

docs.text: What to do next? We had our successful launch. The ARC results have come out and are very similar to last year, with some changes to the body tube diameter requirements, two eggs instead of 1, and a 50ft bump to apogee. Nothing crazy, meaning our current design for apogee control should work well. The main challenge will be somehow combining descent control AND ascent control into one grandiose design that will perfectly qualify for nationals. The main issue, of course, is cable management with the descent control: IMAGE OF SUPER TANGLED CABLES And also the weight. The ARC ascent-control design was barely under the 650g weight cap, and our current reefing project was also in the 600g range. Though a lot of the mass is overlapped (same majority of electronics, motor, 3D printed parts, etc...), there are also unique parts like the humongous 35kg/cm servo that weighs 70 grams on its own. Combining these two electronically controlled designs into one will be excruciatingly difficult, but I believe it can be done. I wish us luck next year and I hope to revisit this documentation soon!

docs.text: Progress Report #2 8/10/26 The most recent progress has been in the form of testing. There have been a few drop tests done with the prototyped design off the 30ft tower, but a huge problem remains. The drop was only about 2 seconds, even fully expanded out - this means that we would need a grossly larger tower in order to see any meaningful differences with the reefing mechanism, or we have to do something with a much higher chance of failure: Sending a rocket up with the mechanism (to an incredibly tall height around 1000ft) and then measuring the much more significant descent time differences there. This will provide much more information but will also need much more development, including the construction of a whole new non-guided rocket and coordinating a launch. Avoiding this would be better but unfortunately we are under a significant time crunch, and we need to know whether this design is even close to working so this may be our only solution. Other problems include the parachute being somewhat fragile - the shroud lines we attached are put into grommets, which have a nonzero chance of tearing through the fabric. Manufactured parachutes have the luxury of advanced threading and gluing techniques to avoid weak joints, which we are (as of yet) unable to replicate and instead have a crude system of additional grommets that we are connecting the shrouds to. Additionally these are some videos testing the parachute lines on the ground with a fan, as a form of 'portable wind tunnel'. These tests had varied success, particularly due to the rotational wind patterns that resulted in the shroud lines slowly twisting. However, they showed with a (somewhat) continous air pressure, 'pulling' in the parachute resulted in a reduction in circumference rather than the parachute just being pulled closer to the rocket. docs.text: Progress Report #3 (final!) We have decided to bite the bullet and construct an entire rocket to test the effectiveness of the reefing design. It would have been much more preferred to use a small-scale prototype, but with significant time constraints (my teammate’s college departure, who's coding has been critical to this project) production has been rushed to making a full rocket with the integrated reefing mechanism. The first step in the construction of this rocket, as always, is to plug in basic parameters into the software OpenRocket, which will calculate/approximate basic stability and apogee details. The most crucial details when designing a basic rocket like this are the weights of individual components (fins, nose cone, ‘mass component’ in the center to represent avionics, etc) and then match them as closely as possible in the real world. This can be achieved through modifying infill and print material with FDM printing. The aerodynamic stability of the rocket, measured in calibers, is approximately 1.52, which is considered well within the ‘sweet spot’ of 1-2 calibers for model rockets to both remain . This value simply measures how many rocket body (body tube) diameters the center of gravity is ahead of the center of pressure. This value is important as it ensures the rocket won’t tumble due to being under stable or ‘weathercock’ (turn into the wind due to stability being too high). The intuitive explanation can be given through this NASA model rocketry diagram: It was quite simple to model all the corresponding parts that are associated with the OpenRocket - making a fin can with the same fin dimensions, a simple nose cone, etc. The body tube is one diameter continuous, that being BT-80 (66mm outer, 65mm inner diam) thus not requiring dubious levels of modeling for a transition piece between the two of them and matching two different diameters. The parts are always modeled with 0.05cm of wiggle room to account for thermal expansion. Once the fin can was modeled, it was printed out of basic PLA and then epoxied onto the body tube, with one half of the shock cord attached to a drill hole within that fin can. It can be noted that the transition looks quite unique, with a 'channel' running down the side and a small hook section that leans into the body of the rocket. This was done intentionally, so that the line of the shock cord would be less tangled with the parachute itself or associated shroud lines prior to the two halves separating from the ejection charge. It also allowed for us to mount the servo in a vertical fashion (with the axis of rotation being in line with the body tubes), as the dimensions of the servo would have made it difficult to fit in any other orientation. To make the string naturally collect on the spool due to gravity, this resulted in a requirement of horizontal feeding. The spool, naturally, has raised edges as to prevent the shock cord from slipping off during winching. Here is the progression of the various winch designs we tried before settling on the final circular design. Due to the size of the servo, the placement of the winch had to be slightly off-center (the drive shaft of the center is not centered, and the servo could not be fit into the BT80 in such a way to make it as such). PHOTOS OF WINCHES I also soldered a simple circuit for this. It has very similar components to our earier "Superova" project. It includes the Arduino Nano Every, the Verter 3-5V Buck Boost (required for the LiPo that provides 3.7V to the operating voltage of 5V on the Nano), 2200 microfarad capacitor (for the servo to not cause severe supply voltage drop from current spike), the classic BMP390 barometric pressure sensor for altitude/velocity/acceleration calculations, and the aforementioned 3.7V LiPO (2000mAh). We also used a small piece of a breadboard in order to wire all of these connections together instead of using wired junctions, as there have been incidents in the past where these connections fail or are difficult to add new components to. It is important to note that an SD reader was not used this time, considered unneeded, so all flight data had to be stored on the on-board EEPROM. For the Nano this is a ridiculously small 256 BYTES, meaning all non-essential information must not be tracked. This meant we only tracked the rockets velocity immediately following the start of the winching (during descent), and did not track altitude on the way up, deemed unecessary for this test. WIRING DIAGRAM PICTURE OF FINISHED WIRING Finally, we had finished all essential parts of this project. A few days before the departure of my close friend, teammate, and lead programmer, on August 15th, we decided to perform a launch. Selfie of both of us in front of car Picture of loaded up car We arrived onto the launch field in Acton, set up the launch rail, and loaded the program onto the Nano. Picture of Nano with cable sticking out and half of the mechanism just out there This is crucial due to the drift that the barometric pressure sensor experiences. Additionally, it is best for the program to be started on the launch site, as the battery does not last forever and the initial temperature benchmark (done by the BMP) should be based on external temp instead of temp inside the car or other location. In short, the final software upload has become a ritual of our launches. And we're off! We set up the rocket on the launch rail, and counted down the seconds to ascertain the summers worth of work following our failure to qualify for ARC. I apologize for the exclamations, I was quite excited to see this launch. VIDEO OF LAUNCH VIDEO OF ROCKET COMING DOWN Though it is difficult to tell from this video, it was far clearer in the field that the parachute slowly experienced radial contraction as the ratio of height of parachute to radius increased.

This value is important as it ensures the rocket won’t tumble due to being under stable or ‘weathercock’ (turn into the wind due to stability being too high). The intuitive explanation can be given through this NASA model rocketry diagram: It was quite simple to model all the corresponding parts that are associated with the OpenRocket - making a fin can with the same fin dimensions, a simple nose cone, etc. The body tube is one diameter continuous, that being BT-80 (66mm outer, 65mm inner diam) thus not requiring dubious levels of modeling for a transition piece between the two of them and matching two different diameters. The parts are always modeled with 0.05cm of wiggle room to account for thermal expansion. Once the fin can was modeled, it was printed out of basic PLA and then epoxied onto the body tube, with one half of the shock cord attached to a drill hole within that fin can. It can be noted that the transition looks quite unique, with a 'channel' running down the side and a small hook section that leans into the body of the rocket. This was done intentionally, so that the line of the shock cord would be less tangled with the parachute itself or associated shroud lines prior to the two halves separating from the ejection charge. It also allowed for us to mount the servo in a vertical fashion (with the axis of rotation being in line with the body tubes), as the dimensions of the servo would have made it difficult to fit in any other orientation. To make the string naturally collect on the spool due to gravity, this resulted in a requirement of horizontal feeding. The spool, naturally, has raised edges as to prevent the shock cord from slipping off during winching. Here is the progression of the various winch designs we tried before settling on the final circular design. Due to the size of the servo, the placement of the winch had to be slightly off-center (the drive shaft of the center is not centered, and the servo could not be fit into the BT80 in such a way to make it as such).

docs.text: I also soldered a simple circuit for this. It has very similar components to our earier "Superova" project. It includes the Arduino Nano Every, the Verter 3-5V Buck Boost (required for the LiPo that provides 3.7V to the operating voltage of 5V on the Nano), 2200 microfarad capacitor (for the servo to not cause severe supply voltage drop from current spike), the classic BMP390 barometric pressure sensor for altitude/velocity/acceleration calculations, and the aforementioned 3.7V LiPO (2000mAh). We also used a small piece of a breadboard in order to wire all of these connections together instead of using wired junctions, as there have been incidents in the past where these connections fail or are difficult to add new components to. It is important to note that an SD reader was not used this time, considered unneeded, so all flight data had to be stored on the on-board EEPROM. For the Nano this is a ridiculously small 256 BYTES, meaning all non-essential information must not be tracked. This meant we only tracked the rockets velocity immediately following the start of the winching (during descent), and did not track altitude on the way up, deemed unecessary for this test.

docs.text: Supernova Year 1 This is the documentation for my first big project, Supernova. Traditionally, the way that my aerospace club has attempted to qualify for ARC has been with the usage of a NG (non-guided) rocket. This means that all altitude control was decided before the rocket was in flight and was purely mass-based. In a vacuum, this idea works great! However, micro-adjustments in wind make huge impacts on rocket apogee, especially with the consistent weight requirement being around ~650g for ARC. One launch can be perfect, and without changing anything the next launch can garner 50 points (which for ARC is already far worse than qualifying standards of ~15 per launch, but preferably closer to 10.) However, I have been told by older members of the club that they've also worked on guided rockets as side projects, yet never attempted to qualify with them. That the system wasn't reliable enough, and it would be better to gamble with a nonguided design and hope that the winds were favorable. But I didn't particularly like that. So, I started brainstorming what I could do. Obviously, the rocket somehow needed a way to control its apogee actively, taking in information from some sort of sensor. But how would it control apogee? The previous years' guided designs had focused around air brakes, which would slide out horizontally from the body of the rocket in a petal-like formation in order to arrest the movement of the rocket. This seemed excruciatingly difficult to model and would likely have unprecedented stability issues. So, I thought the easier solution would be to take a page out of the drag racing book, and use a parachute to slow down the movement of the rocket. This would prove to be far more difficult than I initially thought, but was still likely easier aerodynamics-wise compared to air brakes.
